open-question.question: The recommend-open-question agent becomes an alternatives-only agent dispatched by /provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions and is renamed to match its role. What is its new name (for example provide-alternatives-to-open-question), given that the orchestrator addresses it by its namespaced registry name and five files reference the old one?

The tool needs a partial strip that clears only the recommendation, depends-on, and applied-principle children while keeping the alternatives, and the full strip that clears every child still serves as the hatch for a stale alternative set. Is the partial strip a flag on the existing strip subcommand, a new subcommand, or the new default of strip with the full strip behind a flag?
open-question.alternative: Keep `strip`'s bare form clearing every child and add a mode flag — `strip --recommendation SHORT_TITLE…` — that clears only the `<recommendation>`, `<depends-on>` and `<applied-principle>` children and leaves the `<alternative>` set standing, the same narrowing the cascade applies internally through the one shared per-block primitive. It follows the polarity this tool already establishes, where the bare subcommand is the broad uniform treatment and a flag narrows it — `remove` bare strips every dependent and `--option` narrows, `list` bare prints every block and `--unannotated` narrows — so nothing shipped changes meaning: every existing `strip` call, `test_strip.py`'s pinned strip-to-bare outcome, and every sentence saying strip clears every child stay true and unedited, and `strip --recommendation` reads as the exact mirror of an `embed` that names the same half with the same word. The hatch the new design makes routine — clear a stale recommendation so the inline pass can re-run it — is the longer form, while the rarer and more expensive one is a bare word, so a mistyped `strip` discards an alternative set that cost a parallel agent dispatch.

Invert the subcommand: bare `strip` clears only the recommendation, depends-on and applied-principle children, and the full clear moves behind a flag such as `strip --all`. The bare word does the safe, now-routine thing and the one operation that throws away parallel-dispatch work must be asked for explicitly, so the expensive artifact is guarded by the command form itself rather than by the caller having read the right hatch sentence. It silently redefines a shipped subcommand — same command, no error, different result — so an old chain or a user's muscle memory quietly stops clearing what it cleared, and every `strip` sentence in CLAUDE.md, `docs/`, and the sweep's hatch plus `test_strip.py`'s pinned semantics must be re-pointed in one change, against the tool's own bare-is-broad polarity.

Leave `strip` untouched and add a second verb for the partial clear (for example `unrecommend SHORT_TITLE…`), both implemented over one shared per-block primitive. Each verb carries exactly one meaning and one argparse help text end to end, no flag can be omitted or mistyped, and `strip`'s existing contract, tests, and every sentence describing it stand entirely unchanged. It puts two names in front of one write whose only difference is which child kinds survive — precisely the case this tool spells as a mode flag everywhere else — adding an eleventh verb, its own test file, and a naming question of its own, and reading inconsistently beside an `embed` whose two shapes are named by flags.
open-question.recommendation: Two blast radii for one write is what this tool spells as a flag on the broad bare form, exactly as `remove --option` narrows `remove`, and keeping the full strip as the default leaves every shipped call, test, and sentence about `strip` true while the new flag reads as the mirror of embed's recommendation shape; only if a bare `strip` slip were unrecoverable, rather than one re-dispatch of the alternatives pass, would flipping the default win instead.

open-question.question: The embed subcommand must accept two fragment shapes: alternatives only (from the parallel agent) and recommendation only, with its depends-on and applied-principle children (from the inline recommendation pass). Does the tool tell them apart by inspecting the fragment, or does the caller name the shape with an explicit flag, and what must the target block already hold for each shape (no alternatives yet for the first, alternatives but no recommendation for the second)?
open-question.alternative: One `embed` subcommand whose caller names the shape with a required, mutually exclusive flag pair — `--alternatives` for the parallel pass (sliced between its own first and last `<alternative>` anchor lines, accepted only when the block carries no `<alternative>` yet, the full strip being the hatch) and `--recommendation` for the inline pass (accepted only when the block carries at least one `<alternative>` and no `<recommendation>` yet, the partial strip being the hatch, with the recommendation's `option` validated against the block's own alternative ids since the fragment carries none) — each shape writing only its own child kinds and sharing one validation core. It matches the tool's established one-verb-with-a-mode-flag style (`list --unannotated`, `lift --alternative`, `remove --option`), keeps every call site self-describing about which pass it is, and lets each refusal name both what the pass asked for and what the block holds, while `--recommendation` never touching the `<alternative>` children makes the frozen alternative set a property of the tool rather than of caller discipline. It is the tool's first subcommand with a required argument, the flag restates information the document already determines so it must be kept true at two call sites and in the repair template, and it reads inconsistently if the sibling question "Strip command forms" settles on a second subcommand rather than a flag on `strip`.

`embed` keeps its single call form and decides the shape from the piped message — an `<alternative>` anchor line present means the alternatives shape, its absence with a `<recommendation>` line means the recommendation shape — then applies whichever precondition that shape implies. Nothing new appears at either call site or in the shape-reminder repair template, so the two passes state what to pipe and never what mode to pipe it in. The slice anchors must be chosen before the parse, by substring tests over prose that these very agents write about `<alternative>` elements, and a return carrying both halves is indistinguishable from an intended one, so the recommendation pass could overwrite the frozen alternatives unless the tool infers a shape only to refuse it — the flag's job done blind — and every refusal names what the fragment lacks instead of what the pass expected.

No flag and no fragment guessing: the target block's current children select the shape, because the two preconditions are mutually exclusive and exhaustive over the legal states — a block with no `<alternative>` accepts only an alternatives fragment, a block with alternatives and no `<recommendation>` only a recommendation fragment, and a block with both is refused until one of the strips runs. The shape test and the precondition are one single test, so no flag can ever disagree with the document, nothing is inferred from prose, and both passes keep an identical one-line call form. The caller cannot state its intent, so a block whose alternatives an answer-time cascade cleared silently becomes an alternatives-shape target and the recommendation pass's return is refused for holding no `<alternative>` element — blaming the fragment when the fault is the missing alternative set — and any later third shape breaks the exhaustiveness the whole scheme rests on.

Retire the single `embed` for a pair, `embed-alternatives` and `embed-recommendation`, each with its own positional argument, help text, precondition, refusal strings, and test file. The shape is fixed at the call site and can never be omitted, and each subcommand's argparse help documents exactly one contract end to end. It puts two names in front of one write path whose wrapper-line, well-formedness, stray-text and `<depends-on>` checks are shared, introduces the first two-word subcommand into a vocabulary of single verbs (create, list, locate, lift, add, strip, embed, remove, walk, sort), and re-points every documentation surface that names `embed` today.
open-question.recommendation: Two shapes of one write are exactly what a mode flag expresses in this tool's existing style, and naming the shape lets each refusal cite the pass's expectation alongside the block's state while the preconditions it enforces — no `<alternative>` yet for the alternatives shape, alternatives but no `<recommendation>` for the recommendation shape, whose option is checked against the block's own ids — are what keep the alternative set frozen between passes; only if the recommendation pass ever had to write into a block with no alternatives would block-state selection win instead.

open-question.question: The parallel alternatives pass needs the ids of the blocks that carry no alternative elements, which the existing list --unannotated (no recommendation element) does not express. What is the new list filter called, and does --unannotated keep its current meaning?
open-question.alternative: Retire the `--unannotated` spelling and give `list` two symmetric negative filters named for the child kind each tests — `--without-alternatives` (the parallel pass's dispatch set, and the inline pass's one-call stop test) and `--without-recommendation`, which carries today's semantics unchanged as the recommendation pass's idempotency skip. Each flag states the element it tests, so neither pass's set has to be remembered from a convention, and the same two words name the same two halves across every surface this milestone touches — `embed --alternatives` / `--recommendation` and `strip --recommendation` — while the `without-` prefix keeps a filter's negative polarity explicit where a bare `--alternatives` would read as the blocks that have them; the split is precisely what costs `--unannotated` its single referent, since a block carrying alternatives is annotated yet that filter would still print it. It renames a shipped flag, so the sweep skill, `docs/skill-reference.md`, the two CLAUDE.md entries and the five test files that spell `--unannotated` (`test_list.py`, `test_sort.py`, `test_walk.py`, `test_embed.py`, `test_strip.py`) must be re-pointed in the same change, and the tool's most-called read becomes the wordiest line in both passes.

Leave `--unannotated` exactly as it is — spelling and meaning — and add one new flag beside it for the other half, for example `list --without-alternatives`, so nothing shipped changes. It is strictly additive: every existing call, pinned test assertion and sentence about `--unannotated` stays true and unedited, the recommendation pass keeps the gather line it already runs, and the whole tool diff is one argparse flag, one `cmd_list` branch and one test. The two set-defining filters then rest on different naming principles — one on the element it tests, one on a word the split has just left with two possible referents — so every reader of either skill must carry the convention that annotated means the recommendation half alone, and a later child kind arrives with no pattern to follow.

Give `--unannotated` the new meaning — blocks carrying no `<alternative>`, the wholly bare block the first pass targets — and move today's meaning to a second new flag such as `--unrecommended`. The plainest word then literally names the block with nothing embedded and points at the pipeline's new front, so the filter a user meets first is the one spelled most simply. It is exactly the silent redefinition the sibling `strip` question rejected — same flag, no error, a different set — so every sentence and pinned test naming `--unannotated` is quietly false until re-pointed, it pays for two renames rather than one, and it leaves a pair whose two words differ only by a suffix.

Replace `--unannotated` with one filter that takes the child kind as its value — `list --missing alternatives` and `list --missing recommendation` — over an argparse `choices` list. One flag covers both halves and any later child kind with no further naming question, and because its value is the element name itself the filter can never be read in the wrong polarity. It makes `list` the first read filter with a required value, so a bare `--missing` is an argparse usage error rather than a meaningful call, and it buys extensibility for a format whose two annotation halves this very milestone freezes.
open-question.recommendation: Today's filter keeps its exact meaning and its job as the recommendation pass's idempotency skip but not its spelling, because the split leaves annotated with two referents — a block carrying alternatives is annotated, yet `--unannotated` would still print it — so each filter is named for the element it tests, which also keeps one pair of words meaning one pair of halves across `list`, `embed` and `strip`; only if this flag were typed by users outside this repository, rather than only by the two passes and the test suite, would the additive option's zero churn win instead.

recommend-procedure.md currently produces alternatives and recommendation as one unit and is referenced by the recommend agent and /discuss-open-question. With the alternatives agent needing only the enumeration half, the inline recommendation pass only the pick half, and discuss both, is the shared core split into two shared files or kept as one file with two separately referenceable steps?
open-question.alternative: Split the core into two shared procedures — an enumeration file that the alternatives agent and discuss-open-question follow, and a pick file that the inline recommendation pass and discuss-open-question follow (the pick half can keep the existing recommend-procedure.md path to limit reference churn) — each self-contained with its own grounding step. Each runner loads only the half it acts on, and each grounding step names only that half's inputs: the principle store and the sibling-dependency disclosure duty are pick-half concerns, while the alternatives agent, dispatched in parallel before any sibling carries a recommendation, has none to lean on — and each half has two runners, so both clear the plugin's shared-means-two-or-more-runners bar. The genuinely common grounding discipline (prefer the live project over memory, read requirements.md and open_questions.xml whole for reasoning only) is stated in both files and can drift; discuss-open-question must reference both in order and say when the pick half runs against already-embedded alternatives, wording that depends on how "Discuss with frozen alternatives" settles.

Keep recommend-procedure.md as one file and let each caller name the steps it follows — the alternatives agent grounding plus enumeration, the inline pass grounding plus the pick, discuss-open-question both. One grounding step with nothing duplicated, the smallest edit to a file three runners already reference, and a reader still sees the whole analytical arc in one place. Every runner loads the half it must not act on — the alternatives agent would read a recommend-one step it is forbidden to perform, exactly the bleed the two-pass split exists to prevent — and the per-half divergences (principle store, disclosure duty, frozen alternatives) become conditionals inside shared steps, against the runtime rule that a file holds only what the runner acting on it needs.

Three shared files: one grounding procedure both halves reference, plus an enumeration file and a pick file that each add only their own analytical step. No grounding text is duplicated anywhere while each half still states only its own work. Two hops of reference and three files for what is a 72-line procedure today, each runner still loading two of them so the load-minimality gain is small, and a grounding step alone is too thin to carry the Inputs contract every shared procedure here declares.
open-question.recommendation: Two passes run by different runners at different times are two units of work, and their grounding genuinely diverges — the principle store and the sibling-disclosure duty belong to the pick half alone — so the halves are two texts rather than one duplicated; were the two grounding steps to come out word-for-word identical, the one-file option would win instead.
